body:
Agriculture as the Foundation of Harappan Life

The Harappan or Indus civilisation was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. Its Mature Harappan phase flourished approximately between 2600 BCE and 1900 BCE. Although cities such as Harappa and Mohenjodaro are famous for their planned streets and buildings, these urban centres depended upon agriculture and animal husbandry in the surrounding countryside.

Harappan society included farmers, herders, craftspersons and people engaged in other occupations. Farmers cultivated crops, herders maintained livestock, and settlements obtained additional food through fishing, hunting and gathering. Agricultural production supported people who did not directly produce their own food, including specialised craftspersons working in towns and cities.

Subsistence

Subsistence refers to the means through which people obtain the food and other essential resources needed for survival. Harappan subsistence combined crop cultivation, livestock rearing, fishing, hunting and gathering.

Major Crops Cultivated by the Harappans

The Harappans cultivated several cereals, pulses and oilseeds. Remains of grains and seeds show that agriculture was diverse rather than dependent upon a single crop.

Crop categoryImportant examplesSignificance
CerealsWheat and barleyImportant food grains in the Harappan agricultural economy
Other cerealsMillets and riceMillets were important at several Gujarat sites; rice remains are relatively uncommon
PulsesLentils, chickpeas and peasProvided additional plant-based food
OilseedsSesame, mustard and linseedProvided oil-bearing seeds and other useful products
Fibre cropCottonSupplied fibre for spinning and textile production

Wheat and Barley

Wheat and barley were important cereals cultivated in the Harappan region. Both are suited to cultivation during the cooler growing season in many parts of northwestern India. Their presence demonstrates the importance of established agricultural practices in supporting Harappan settlements.

The occurrence of these crops at a site does not necessarily mean that they were the only cereals cultivated there. Harappan agriculture varied according to local rainfall, soils and water availability.

Millets and Rice

Millets were particularly significant in parts of Gujarat, where their remains have been identified at Harappan settlements. Several millet varieties are comparatively well suited to cultivation under seasonal rainfall and relatively dry conditions.

Evidence from Gujarat shows that agricultural practices could differ substantially from those in the main Indus plains. At some Gujarat settlements, millets formed an important part of the crop economy.

Rice was known in parts of the Harappan world, but its remains are relatively rare compared with those of wheat and barley. Rice remains have been reported from Gujarat sites including Lothal and Rangpur. Therefore, it is incorrect to describe rice as either entirely unknown to the Harappans or as their principal cereal.

Pulses and Oilseeds

Pulses such as lentils, chickpeas and peas increased the variety of plant foods available to Harappan communities. Sesame, mustard and linseed were also cultivated. These crops could supplement cereals and provide useful seeds, including those containing oil.

Different crops had different requirements for moisture, temperature and growing conditions. Cultivating several types of crops helped communities make use of locally available agricultural resources.

Regional Variation in Agriculture

Harappan settlements extended across regions with different climates and environments. Consequently, the crops cultivated in one area were not necessarily identical to those grown elsewhere.

The Indus plains supported substantial cultivation of wheat and barley. In Gujarat, archaeological evidence demonstrates the importance of millets alongside other crops. The Harappan settlement of Khirsara in Kachchh has yielded evidence of crops including wheat, barley, millets, pulses, sesame and cotton.

This regional variation is important because the Harappan civilisation was a large cultural region, not a single agricultural village operating under uniform environmental conditions.

How Agriculture Supported Cities

Urban settlements contained specialised workers who needed a dependable food supply. Agricultural production in villages and rural settlements helped sustain these populations.

Agricultural surplus means produce remaining after cultivators meet their immediate needs, including food and seed requirements. Such surplus could support non-farming occupations. This relationship helps explain how sizeable urban settlements and specialised crafts could develop within the Harappan civilisation.

However, the precise arrangements through which agricultural produce was collected, distributed or exchanged are not fully known. The presence of cities demonstrates the need for organised food supply, but it does not establish a particular taxation system or method of payment.

Prelims focus

  • Wheat and barley were important Harappan cereals.
  • Millets were significant at several Gujarat settlements.
  • Rice remains are relatively rare but have been reported from Harappan sites.
  • Lentils, chickpeas, peas, sesame, mustard and linseed were among the cultivated crops.
  • Cotton was an important fibre crop associated with textile production.
  • Trap: The Harappan agricultural economy was not restricted to wheat and barley, and crop patterns were not identical throughout the civilisation.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 2–3; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 38–39; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 96–97; A. K. Pokharia, J. S. Kharakwal and A. Srivastava, Archaeobotanical Evidence of Millets in the Indian Subcontinent, Journal of Archaeological Science, vol. 42, 2014, pp. 442–455.]

title: Harappan Agriculture: Crops, Food Production and the Urban Economy

body:
Agricultural Implements and Cultivation

Crop cultivation requires preparing the soil, sowing seeds, protecting crops and harvesting the produce. The Harappans possessed agricultural knowledge and implements suitable for these activities. The plough was one of their important agricultural implements.

A plough loosens and turns the upper layer of soil, making it easier to prepare land for sowing. Wooden ploughs generally decay over time, so the strongest evidence for Harappan ploughing comes from surviving models and the remains of cultivated fields rather than preserved wooden ploughs.

Kalibangan: Evidence of a Ploughed Field

Kalibangan in Rajasthan is especially important for evidence of ancient agriculture. A ploughed field has been identified there in an Early Harappan context.

The field contained 2 sets of furrows running approximately at right angles to one another. This arrangement suggests that different crops may have been cultivated together in the same field.

The interpretation is that the intersecting furrows could accommodate crops with different spacing requirements. The evidence establishes a distinctive cultivation pattern, but the precise crops planted in those particular furrows cannot be identified merely from their arrangement.

Kalibangan, Rajasthan: evidence of a ploughed field with 2 intersecting sets of furrows, associated with the Early Harappan period.

Banawali: A Terracotta Plough Model

A terracotta model of a plough has been discovered at Banawali in present-day Haryana. Terracotta means clay that has been shaped and hardened by firing.

The model provides evidence that the plough was known in Harappan society. Similar models have also been reported from Cholistan, in present-day Pakistan.

The discoveries at Kalibangan and Banawali should be distinguished carefully. Kalibangan is associated with an actual ploughed field, whereas Banawali is associated with a model of the agricultural implement.

Use of Oxen

Terracotta figures and seal representations show that cattle, including bulls, were familiar to the Harappans. Oxen were probably used to draw ploughs and may also have helped in transporting goods.

The use of oxen for ploughing is a reasonable reconstruction based on the available evidence. It should not be confused with the direct discovery of a complete wooden plough and its associated draught animals in a field.

Need for Irrigation

Many Harappan settlements were located in semi-arid regions where rainfall was limited or seasonal. Agriculture therefore depended upon effective use of natural water sources, soil moisture and, in some places, supplementary irrigation.

Irrigation

Irrigation is the artificial supply of water to agricultural land when natural rainfall or available soil moisture is insufficient for crop growth.

Canals at Shortughai

Shortughai in Afghanistan has yielded traces of canals associated with a Harappan settlement. This is an important example of possible irrigation infrastructure.

Comparable canal remains have not been identified at the major Harappan sites in Punjab and Sind in the same way. Ancient channels may have disappeared or become covered by sediments, but their possible existence should not be treated as established evidence.

It would therefore be incorrect to conclude that a uniform, extensive canal-irrigation network served every Harappan city.

Wells and Local Water Sources

Wells provided an important means of obtaining groundwater in Harappan settlements. Water drawn from wells may also have been used for irrigation in some areas.

Rivers, seasonal streams and the moisture retained in floodplains could also support cultivation. The relative importance of these sources varied from settlement to settlement.

Dholavira: Water Management in Gujarat

Dholavira was located on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kachchh, Gujarat. Its surroundings were relatively dry, and reliable water supply was a major requirement for sustaining the settlement.

The inhabitants developed an elaborate system of reservoirs and channels to collect, store and manage water. Seasonal streams supplied water that could be directed into storage facilities.

Some reservoirs were built with stone masonry, while others were partly cut into rock. These installations demonstrate that the Harappans could adapt their water-management techniques to local environmental conditions.

Dholavira's reservoirs were important for water storage and settlement needs. Their possible use for agriculture is also relevant, but the existence of reservoirs does not prove that every reservoir was constructed specifically for crop irrigation.

Adaptation to Different Environments

Harappan agricultural practices were influenced by rainfall, river systems, soil conditions and the availability of water. Settlements in riverine plains could benefit from river water and fertile soils, whereas settlements in drier regions required greater attention to water collection and conservation.

The importance of millets in Gujarat also shows that different communities cultivated crops suited to their local conditions. Such regional adaptations helped support settlements across the extensive Harappan cultural area.

Prelims focus

  • Kalibangan: Early Harappan ploughed field with 2 sets of intersecting furrows.
  • Banawali: terracotta model of a plough.
  • Shortughai: traces of canals.
  • Dholavira: reservoirs and sophisticated water-management arrangements.
  • Oxen were probably used for ploughing.
  • Trap: Evidence of canals at Shortughai does not establish a universal Harappan canal-irrigation system.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 3–4, section 2.1, Agricultural Technologies; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, p. 38; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, pp. 95–96; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Criterion (iv), accessed 17 November 2026.]
